title: Setup and orientation
oneConcept: 3D multiplies what you already know in 2D.

beats.retrievalHook:
Welcome back from summer, everyone!! It's our first week together, so there's no homework. Our only goal is to ensure we're all on the same page.

This first assignment is an in-class exercise, not take-home work, so there's nothing to catch up on afterward. This week is worth 5% of your overall grade, added on top after the end-of-semester tally, so it's a real chance to push past 100%! Go for it.

If you are comfortable with everything already, then perfect! We will have a page dedicated to Blender Shortcuts and Navigation below. The purpose of this week is to introduce you to the visual development, and this class will focus you in on related 3D techniques you'll benefit from.
beats.oneNewConcept:
**3D multiplies what you already know in 2D.**

The word to hold onto all term is *study*, not *final*, because a study is allowed to be rough, and rough is exactly what we expect. Nothing has to be finished, it just has to be *decidable*, so we can tell which direction is worth keeping.

We make iterations and variations of the same subject, and the skill is doing it with efficiency: block it, try three directions, drop two, keep one, move on. A rough read beats a perfect one, because the eye lands on the look, not the UVs, and the art director never sees the UVs. Our day-to-day job is finding the right look for our show, and that's the craft that carries you into any industry, because the fundamentals don't change.

So this term we build toward the basics: **modeling, lighting, and rendering.** Those three are the core of a visual developer's work, and they work the same way whether you're in games, film, advertising, or products. Get them solid and you can point at any job in any industry and say, I've got the basics for that!

And here's what that looks like as a semester: three main projects. The exact specs may shift with how the term goes, but the shape of it won't change, and I'm excited for all of it!

- **3 blockouts of a room**, the same place in three different directions
- **3 variations of the same prop or character**, one subject, three reads
- **a 4-panel sequence**, a small story told in four frames

Today's Demo

We're going to open a starter scene and go through the naming conventions that will carry you through the semester, and I'll show you tools that will help you make your Blender experience easier! File organization is just as important as design skill. The starter scene has collections with names a person can read, a camera and a light rig that's already set up, and a render engine that's already in a sensible place. The tool does the setup, so your time goes to decisions, not to wiring. You don't have to remember any of it, just let it land, and ask, because I'd much rather answer a question than watch someone wrestle a panel.

> **Aside (further reading):** *The Complete Guide to Blender Graphics, Volume 1* by Blain, the interface and viewport chapters. It's a recent edition, so it sits closest to the current layout. Good for your "where is that" moments, just let it answer the questions, no need to read it as a project.
beats.guidedMaking:
This week we get on the same page and gear into our 3D VisDev workflow. Here's the one thing we make, and we take it all the way through: pick one object, a treasure chest, a table, a chair, or a bottle, model it, add materials to it, light a room, place a camera, name everything properly, and render it. That's the deliverable, and it stays small on purpose!

1. **Pick your subject.** Choose one, a treasure chest, a table, a chair, or a bottle. That single choice is your subject for the whole pass, so pick the one you can see the clearest idea of, and stay with it.
2. **Set up a clean file.** Open the Starter Scene and just *look* before you touch anything. Name the collections: `00_world`, `10_set`, `20_light`, `30_cam`. Where's the camera, where are the lights, where would you put your own work? If the naming isn't clear to you, that's a useful thing to notice, not a problem.
   - *Manual fallback:* no Starter Scene? No worries. Start from a fresh file and build the same structure by hand. Four collections: `00_world`, `10_set`, `20_light`, `30_cam`. Add one camera and a key/fill/rim from the lamp menu. Same result, just a few more clicks. Both ways work.
3. **Model it.** Build it from simple shapes. Give it a believable proportion, the size and mass of the thing you're after. Don't add detail, add intent.
4. **Add materials.** Put a base color and a roughness on the surfaces so the object reads as something made of something. A treasure chest reads wood and metal, a bottle reads glass, a chair reads whatever you commit to. You're not texturing for a final, you're giving the object a surface the light can read.
5. **Light a room.** One key light and a soft fill, placed so your subject reads with a little shape to it. You're testing whether the light gives the object a face, not chasing a perfect look.
6. **Place a camera.** Frame your subject the way you'd frame a person: one clean composition, the object reading clearly in the frame.
7. **Render it.** One still render. That's the whole thing, and it's yours!
8. **Save a clean file.** Name it like a person: `a-environment_wk1-setup.blend`, not `scene.blend` or `final_final2.blend`. I see those, I understand them, and we're retiring them this term. Make sure the collections have no orphan junk, and that you can close the file, reopen it, and it still makes sense.

That's the full pipeline on a simple subject, and every week this term builds on it. By the end of the term you'll be doing far more than this, and this is the week that makes it all legible!
beats.check:
No project checkpoint this week. There's just one thing I'd love to know, and you can tell me in your own words:

**Can you open the file, find the one thing you want, and save a clean, well-named file, all on your own?**

If yes, we're all set, and that's a real win for a setup week! If it took a little nudging, that's exactly what the week is for. The file is the thing you're handing in, and the thing is clean. You don't have to be impressive, just able to find your way back in.
beats.reflect:
Here's a recap of today's lesson:

- **What we did:** we set up a clean file and ran the full pass, your object, the room lighting, the camera, clean naming, and a render.
- **What we learned:** 3D makes a good idea fast, it doesn't make a weak idea good, so the grade is on the thinking.
- **What we'd try next:** reopening the file from cold and finding the camera in under ten seconds, so the naming works for a stranger, not just for us.

**Checklist, the things worth not forgetting:**

- Big-picture changes beat perfect polish. The look is what gets judged, so spend the time there.
- Rough is fine at the study stage. A rough read you can decide on beats a perfect one you can't.
- This week's deliverable is the full pass: your object, a lit room, a camera, clean naming, and a render, all in a well-named file.
- Before Week 2, give Project A's brief (the "a" project, at [#/projects/a](#/projects/a)) a quiet read, so the world is already in your head when we start shaping it.

That organization is not busywork, it's the thing that carries you through the whole semester. The same clean file you built today is the one you'll open in Week 8 and still understand, and it's the reason the end-of-term work, the hero renders, the sequences, and the final delivery, is something we can actually do. A well-organized file makes the big work possible! So keep naming like a person, keep the collections tidy, and you'll be in great shape from here on out.

title: Blocking our room
oneConcept: A room is a comparison to a body, and a home for the eye.

beats.retrievalHook:
Welcome back! This week, we'll learn about the three things that make a good blockout: a room's purpose, its scale, and its shape hierarchy. That's the first part of Project A, where we block one room and show it three ways.

For a fast challenge, just imagine what sort of room you'd like to build. Hold the picture for a minute; it comes back when we pick our themes in a few minutes.
beats.oneNewConcept:
**A room is a comparison to a body, and a home for the eye.**

Last week we learned to design for the eye: the look is what gets judged, and a rough read you can decide on beats a perfect one. This week we build on that directly, because a room only works when it gives that same eye a size to read and a place to land on.

A blockout with nothing in it is a box, but the moment a person lands in it, we're building a room. Your brain reads size by comparison. A door next to a figure tells you the height, and a table tells you the scale of everything on it. Without that anchor, your grand library can read as a hallway, and your hallway can read as a cathedral, and you won't know which one you built until you put a body in it. That's all scale is: a comparison, placed on purpose.

So let's give the room a real anchor. Grab the mannequin file from the sidebar and drop it into your scene as your scale reference; it's a human figure, so it already has proportions your eye trusts. Then build the room around it in 3D, and let the space react to the body it's holding. The figure is the truth, and the room is what you adjust.

That anchor is one part of our blockout, and there are three in all. Keep these three in mind, because they are the whole of a good blockout:

- **Purpose:** what the room is for. It's the first thing to decide, because everything else leans on it.
- **Scale:** the size that reads. A room is a comparison to a body, and the figure is the anchor you hang it on.
- **Shape hierarchy:** the one spot the eye lands on. Everything points at it, and everything else steps back.

Scale is the one we just did. Purpose is what the room is for, and it's the first thing to decide, because everything else leans on it. Here are three reads you can pick from. One room is about the path, a route the eye travels through the space from one end to the other. Another is about the destination that's out of reach, a focal point you can see but can't quite get to, like a text on a high shelf or a skylight above you. A third is about the destination that's in reach, a focal point you can reach and interact with, a desk you can sit at, a book you can open. Pick whichever one your room is actually for; that choice is the purpose.

Shape hierarchy is the last part, and it's what keeps the eye from going to die. A space that's the right size but has no point is even, and even is where the eye gets lost. Everything is equally available, so nothing is. Hierarchy is how you end that. You pick the one thing that matters, you make it the strongest value or the clearest shape, and you build a path from the edge of the frame to it. Think of a stage. There's one actor in focus, and the lighting, the set, and everyone else all point at them. The audience's eye isn't allowed to wander. It's walked, hand in hand, to the one spot that matters. Your environment is that stage, and the focal point is the lead actor.

And shape hierarchy has a body to it, because a place is built in sizes. The massing is the large, medium, and small volumes that give the space a body. The big walls and the floor are the large. The desks, the columns, the low plinths are the medium. The one small thing at the focal point, the text, the lamp, the figure, is the small. A place with only large masses is a cave. A place with only small masses is a cluttered table. The mix is what makes it a place. And running through all three of those sizes is value contrast, the bright, mid, dark structure your eye reads at a glance. Put your strongest value on the focal point, and the space stops being a set of shapes and starts being a read.

So that's our blockout, with its three parts: purpose for what the room is for, scale for the size that reads, and shape hierarchy for the one spot the eye lands on. That's the first real design decision of Project A, so it's the one everything else stands on!

**Designing for light**

We're not lighting the scene this week, but we're setting it up so next week's light lands on purpose! Two things we shape now: the shapes and edges that will catch or throw cast shadows once a light is in, and the colour. Colour is a guide for the eye, and the contrast in **value, hue, and saturation** is what carves a path from the edge of the frame to the focal point. The blockout isn't just size and place, it's the stage we're building for the light.

Today's Demo

We'll drop a simple human figure into a rough block of our room and watch the space change its mind. Too small, we feel trapped. Too big, we feel lost. Then we'll add three things, one at a time, and watch the eye stop wandering. First, the massing: a large wall, a medium shelf, a small thing at the point. Second, a strong value on the focal spot, the brightest or darkest thing in the scene, on purpose. Third, a line that points at it, a wall, a path, a row of shelves. Three steps, one result: the space now reads and it leads. That's our blockout in miniature, built from small decisions.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Figure Drawing: Design and Invention* by Michael Hampton, **Chapter 1, "Gesture Drawing."** The reason a human figure is the cleanest scale anchor in the scene is that it already has proportions. The eight-part figure is a known quantity your eye trusts. You don't have to invent its size, so it's the perfect thing to hang the room on.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Framed Ink: Drawing and Composition for Visual Storytellers* by Marcos Mateu-Mestre, **Chapter 3, "The Visual Message within a Still Composition."** A quick read is a composition you can take in at a glance, and that's exactly what your focal point is for. It's the single most useful chapter in that book for this project, and it's short.
beats.guidedMaking:
This week we block our room, and we block it three ways. One goal: **one room, shown as three variations, each reading as the right size, the right place, with the eye going somewhere on purpose.** We gear straight into the VisDev workflow, and this is the first real blockout of the term, so let's make it count!

1. **Pick your theme, then its three designs.** Choose one of these three theme starting points, and within it pick the three room types that become your three variations, one design per variation. Each theme is a self-contained block: its world, then the designs that live inside it. Pick the theme you can see the clearest idea of, then the three designs you can commit to.
   - **Theme 1: The House of Wisdom, Baghdad** (the archive). Warm interior light, paper and ink, reading niches.
     - the round library (a rare text on a plinth at the center)
     - the translation school (a long room of desks, the teacher's desk as the point)
     - the bazaar corner (a scholar's cart among the trade)
     - the canalside study (a waterside nook, the water as the point)
   - **Theme 2: Samarkand, Timurid era** (the blue square). Cobalt and turquoise tilework, high-contrast light, one great square holding many functions.
     - the Registan square (one great open space, a single madrasa facade as the mass)
     - the madrasa courtyard (an enclosed study courtyard, a calligraphy desk at the center)
     - the tilework bazaar (a covered lane, one glowing shopfront under the blue)
     - the domed observatory (a high room with an oculus, the sky as the point)
   - **Theme 3: Timbuktu** (the earth library). Mud-brick and rammed earth, warm low-contrast light, a city that keeps its memory.
     - the Sankore hall (a great lecture hall, the manuscript shelf as the point)
     - the toron mosque (a courtyard of the great mosque, the timber beams as the mass)
     - the river market (the Niger-edge trading ground, one stall lit against the dust)
     - the manuscript room (a small vaulted room of scrolls, one open book as the point)
2. **Drop in the anchor, per variation.** Grab the mannequin file from the sidebar and put one into each of your three variations, in the spot where the beat happens. A low-poly stand-in from the allow-list works just as well.
   - *Manual fallback:* no stand-in model? Model a rough figure yourself. A box for the torso, a sphere for the head, two cylinders for the legs. The anatomy doesn't matter. The height does. Aim for about 1.7 to 1.8 meters and let the space react to it.
3. **Block the massing in three sizes, per variation.** Large (walls, floor, the big volumes), medium (desks, columns, plinths), and the one small thing at your focal point. Big shapes only. No detail, no bevels, no textures. If you're tempted to add a decorative arch, hold it. This week is about size and place, and beauty comes later.
4. **Test the scale, per variation.** Move the figure closer, farther, and to the center. Watch the space change its mind. If it reads too big, bring the walls in. If it reads too small, do the opposite. The figure is the truth, and the room is what you adjust.
5. **Name the focal point, per variation.** The table where the rare text lands. The opening to the sky. The figure in the center. Say it before you touch a light, because the point has to come from the beat, and that beat comes from the purpose you picked.
6. **Make it the strongest, and build the path.** Give each focal point the most value contrast in that variation, the brightest spot or the darkest, on purpose. Then add one or two elements that point at it, a line of shelves, a walkway, a row of repeating shapes. The line doesn't have to be literal. The eye follows lines the way a hand follows a rail.
7. **Cut one competitor, per variation.** Find the one shape that's stealing the eye from the focal point, and remove it or dim it. Hierarchy is as much about what you leave out as what you keep. That cut is a decision, and it's the one we'll ask you to defend at the gate.
8. **Save a clean, named file.** `a-environment_wk2-a1.blend`, with your three variations in clean collections and nothing orphaned. This is the file for A1, so keep it organized now and it stays organized later.

The point of the three variations is that each one is a different decision. Same room, three different ways to read it. One might be tight and intimate, one open and grand, one quiet and one loud. That spread is the whole point, and it's what makes a blockout a study and a study a decision!

**The on-hand tool:** the Starter Scene keeps your collections and naming clean while you block, and its light rig lets you lay down the value contrast at the focal point. If it's not there, build the collection structure by hand and hang a key light on the focal point. The requirement doesn't change.
beats.check:
This is a working-artifact gate. Bring a blockout that already has a sense of scale and a path the eye can walk. It does not need to be pretty. It needs to be decided!

**Pass question:** does this read as a place with a beat, or as a thing in a room?

**Self-check before you show us (answer these, then bring them):**

1. Where is the focal point in each of your three variations, and what pulls the eye there, the light, a line, a size jump? Name one per variation.
2. What is the one thing you would cut to make the beat land harder, in the variation where it's weakest?
3. If we dropped a human in for scale, does the space feel right, too big, or too small? What gives it away?

If you can answer all three, you pass. If you can answer two, we work the third together in the next few minutes, and that work becomes your iteration evidence, not a penalty. That's the deal on every gate this term.
beats.reflect:
Here's a recap of today's lesson:

- **What we did:** we blocked our room at human scale, gave it a purpose and a focal point and an eye path, and cut one competitor, in three different variations.
- **What we learned:** a good blockout has three parts, a purpose for what the room is for, a scale that reads, and a shape hierarchy that gives the eye one place to land.
- **What we'd try next:** moving the figure to a second spot and cutting a second competitor, to see if the beat lands harder, because the first cut was probably the obvious one.

**Checklist, the things worth not forgetting:**

- Big-picture changes beat perfect polish. The look is what gets judged, so spend the time there.
- Rough is fine at the study stage. A rough read you can decide on beats a perfect one you can't.
- This week's deliverable is the blockout: one room, three variations, each with a scale anchor, a purpose, a focal point, and an eye path, all in a well-named file.

That's our blockout, and it's the first real design decision of Project A. A room that reads as the right size, with the eye going somewhere on purpose, is the thing every light, every material, and every camera in the term will stand on. Get it solid and the rest of the project builds on a foundation instead of a guess. That's why we're doing this, and it's the week that makes everything after it legible!
beats.revisit:
Scale is the brick we're laying this week, and it's going to keep coming back. In Project B it decides whether your subject reads as grand or as a hallway. In Project C it decides whether a camera feels motivated or just parked. Same muscle, new tool each time. You've met it once in the voice, and now you've met it in your own file.

**Next week is Week 3, and it's Checkpoint A2.** We take this blocked place and make it read, light, materials, palette, pushed in genuinely different directions. That's make it read, and the test is the one that runs the whole term: are these different decisions, or the same render five times? You'll build them with the Quick Sheet, and you'll learn to kill four of them fast. Bring the A1 file, because the studies are built on it. That's the next door we walk through, and we're looking forward to it!

---

*And one last thing before you head off. If your space reads even and your eye wanders, that's the space asking to be directed. Give it an anchor, a focal point, three sizes, and a value, and it will start telling a story. And if a light won't do what you want, that's a position question, not a you thing. Ask, and we'll sort it out. See you next week.*

title: Project A: light, materials, palette
oneConcept: make it read. Light, materials, and palette as one decision, made in *different* directions.

beats.retrievalHook:
Two questions on last week, then a fast push.

- Block the place had four parts. Name the move you're proudest of, the anchor, the focal point, the massing, or the cut. And what's the *one* thing in your space that's still the wrong size?
- You made the focal point the strongest value. If I moved that focal point to the opposite corner, what would you have to change in the path and the value to keep it landing? Walk me through it, don't build it.

**Fast challenge (2 min):** take your A1 blockout and, in your head, give it a *night* version. Don't model anything. Just tell me: where does the light come from now, what color is it, and does the focal point still read? If the focal point survives a change of light, the hierarchy is real. If it vanishes, the hierarchy was hiding in a lucky daytime setup, and we're about to find out.
beats.oneNewConcept:
**The idea: make it read. Light, materials, and palette as one decision, made in *different* directions.**

Here's the thing a blockout can't do. It holds a person and it points somewhere, but it's still a *shape in space*. To make it read as a place, three systems have to agree. **Light** does the work first: **ambient occlusion** is the soft darkening where shapes meet, and it's what makes a corner feel like a corner. **Cast shadows** are where a form says it has weight and a source. **Highlights** tell you what a surface is made of. And **rim light**, that bright edge where a form separates from the background, is the cheapest way to say *this is a solid thing, not a card*. Get it? Those four are not settings. They're the sentences the light is speaking, and if the focal point can't be heard under them, the hierarchy from last week was a fluke.

Then **materials**. A material is the subject's answer to *what is this made of, and why should I trust it*. In Blender it lives in the **Principled BSDF**, and the two sliders that do most of the work are **roughness** and **base color**. A rough surface diffuses the light and reads soft and used. A smooth one catches it and reads clean and new. So a lamp in tarnished brass reads as *lived-in*, and the same lamp in clean white plastic reads as *just made*. One of them serves your beat and one of them doesn't. That's a material *direction*, and it's a decision, not a default.

And the trap, and it's the one I catch every single time. A student makes one render that's good, then nudges the light a little, turns the camera a little, shifts the tint a little, and now they have four renders. They feel like range. They are the same picture, five times, wearing different hats. The eye can tell. And you can tell. The fix is to change a *whole system*, not a parameter. A direction is a decision about *the whole*. A daytime, warm, wide, grounded read. A nighttime, cool, tight, tense read. A golden-hour, mid, story-driven read. Each one moves light *and* material *and* palette together, because they're one mood, not three knobs. right? A knob is a parameter. A mood is a direction. That's the difference, and it's the whole of A2.

**Why it matters this project:** a *location as a story beat* is only as strong as the best beat you can get out of it. If you only have one mood, you're betting the entire project on that one mood being right. If you have three genuine directions, you can *pick* the one that serves the beat, and that's a design decision you can defend in a room full of people who are going to ask *why* that one and not the other two. That's the 60/40 tilt doing its job. The thinking, not the rendering, is what carries you.

**The demo:** I'll take one blockout and push it in two genuinely different directions, changing light, material, and palette together. First, a warm, wide, grounded read, the library at midday, a rough used material, the eye walking in. Second, a cool, tight, tense read, the same room at night, the material reading darker and smoother, the palette pulling back. And you'll watch the *space* stay the same while the *story* flips. That's direction. Same bricks, different building. get it?

> **Aside (further reading):** *Color and Light* by James Gurney, **Chapter 4, "Light and Form."** The form principle is the idea that light reveals shape, and that's exactly why changing the light changes the read. The directional setups in that chapter are a good list of moods to pick from, warm/cool, hard/soft, high-key/low-key, so you have a vocabulary for the direction instead of guessing. It's a stable idea, so which edition you have doesn't matter much here.

> **Aside (further reading):** *How to Render: The Fundamentals of Light and Shadow and Reflectivity* by Scott Robertson and Thomas Bertling, **Chapter 2, "Light Types and Casting Shadows."** The hard/soft, rim, and occlusion vocabulary is the same vocabulary your focal point uses to stand out. A strong cast shadow or a rim of light on the focal form is a cheap, fast way to say *look here*. A 1-2-3 read, bright, mid, dark, the Chapter 3a idea, is the fastest way to check whether a direction actually *reads* or just looks pretty. Worth a pass before A2.

> **Aside (further reading):** *3D Environment Design with Blender* by Abdelilah Hamdani, **Chapter 2, "The Basics of Realistic Texturing in Blender."** The base-color, roughness, and metallic ideas are the vocabulary for *why* a surface reads as one material or another. Roughness in particular does most of the work, a rough surface diffuses the light and a smooth one catches it, and that's the difference between a default and a decision. It's a recent edition, so closer to 5.x than the older books. Use it for the reasoning, not as a click map.
beats.guidedMaking:
Take your A1 blockout and make it read, in **three to five directional studies**. One goal: **genuinely different decisions, not the same render five times.**

1. **Write the directions first.** Before you touch a light, write one line each. What's the time of day, what's the material reading, what's the palette doing. If you can't write the line, the direction isn't real yet, and that's fine, keep writing until it is.
2. **Build direction one.** Set the light (key, fill, rim, and the occlusion you get for free), the material direction, and the base palette together. Render it. Then stop. This is your baseline from A1, so make sure it's the *strongest* of the set, not the first.
3. **Build direction two, a genuine change.** Change all three at once. If one was warm, wide, and rough, make this one cool, tight, and smooth. Move the light, shift the material, push the palette. If you find yourself only moving the light, you've made a parameter, not a direction. Go back.
4. **Build direction three, and four or five if you have time.** The middle read, or the one that serves the beat best. This is often the winner, but only if the others are strong enough to make the choice mean something. If they're weak, three wins by default, and that's the trap.
5. **Lay them on the Quick Sheet and pick.** Put the renders side by side. Pick the one that serves the beat, and write *why* in one sentence, *why this one and not the others*. That sentence is the artifact. The render is just the proof. Save them all, and name the file `a-environment_wk3-a2.blend`.

beats.oneNewConcept:
**The idea: the hero render, and the paintover that proves you can see past it.**

Here's the thing about a hero render. It's the one you *commit to*. Not the best of five, the one you defend. And the reason the paintover exists is that a 3D render will always have a few places where the tool did the right thing technically and the wrong thing artistically, and the paintover is where you fix those, in a 2D pass over the image. It's the moment where your gate, your drawing and color sense, takes over from your multiplier, the tool. right? The render is the multiplier. The paintover is the gate. Both have to be good, but only one of them is *you*.

Think of it like a photograph and a retouch. A great photo that's never retouched still has the few spots that don't work, a stray highlight, a flat mid, a line that should be softer. A retouch doesn't fix a bad photo, and that's the whole point. It takes a *good* photo and makes it *decided*. Your paintover is the same. It doesn't rescue a weak render, and it shouldn't have to. It takes your chosen direction and tightens the two or three spots that were holding back, and in doing so it shows me, and shows you, that you can *see* the picture, not just produce it. get it?

And the **mood board** is the third piece, and it's not decoration. It's the palette, the references, and the three to five swatches that say *why this look*. Because a hero render without a board is a picture with no argument, and at the crit the first question is always *why this one*. The board is where the answer lives, pulled together before you had to say it out loud.

**Why it matters this project:** a location as a story beat is only finished when someone can say *what it's about* in one sentence. The hero render is the picture. The paintover is the sentence. The board is the argument. Because to paint over a render, you have to know *what to fix and why*, and that's the same skill as defending the whole project. The 60/40 tilt lands here, on the thinking, not the rendering, and the paintover and the board are the proof that the thinking is real. That's the gate between Project A and the rest of the term.

**The demo:** I'll take a decent render and do a live paintover in a 2D app, and I want you to watch my *thinking*, not my brush. I'll point to a spot, say *why* it's not working, and fix it, and I'll do it in three passes, not twenty. First I fix the value structure, the 1-2-3 read. Second I fix the focal point, make it stronger. Third I fix the palette, push the mood. Three passes, one decision each. Then I'll lay the board down, the swatches from the render, a reference or two, and the one line that says what it's about. That's the discipline. A paintover that's twenty random brush strokes is just noise on top of a render, and I'll tell you the difference when I see it, because it shows.

title: Project B: the funpack and turnaround
oneConcept: the funpack workflow, a three-view turnaround that proves the subject holds together.

beats.retrievalHook:
Two questions on the last project, then a fast block.

- In Project A the focal point was the truth and the shapes were what you adjusted. In Project B the *subject* is the truth. What does that flip change about how you'll block it?

**Fast challenge (2 min):** sketch your subject as a *lump*. No detail, no lines, just the overall shape. A bean, a box, a teardrop. Now rotate that lump in your head to the side, and then to the back. Does it still read? If the lump reads from three sides, the subject is real. If it only reads from the front, it's a costume, not a subject, and we're about to find out which one it is. right?
beats.oneNewConcept:
**The idea: the funpack workflow, a three-view turnaround that proves the subject holds together.**

Here's the trap that eats every character or prop in this course. The front is good, because you *designed* the front. The side is a guess, because you never looked at it. The back is a surprise, because you never built it. And the moment a subject has to turn, walk, or be seen from behind, the guess and the surprise show up, and suddenly your beautiful front is attached to a shape that doesn't work. That's the whole reason the funpack exists. It forces you to build the subject *all the way around* before you're allowed to love the front. get it?

The analogy is a sculpture, not a picture. A picture is one face. A sculpture is every face, and the test is whether it holds when you walk around it. Your subject is a sculpture that has to live in a scene that will eventually rotate around it, so if it only works from one angle, it's not a subject, it's a *cardboard cutout* that happens to have a nice front. That's the difference, and the three-view turnaround is how you find out which one you've built.

**Why it matters this project:** a *subject that leads but doesn't trap* (your Project B brief) only leads if it can *be looked at* from wherever the camera ends up. If the back is a mess, the camera can't go behind it, and the subject has a wall it can't cross. If the side is a guess, the subject can't profile, and a profile is half of how a subject *reads*. So the turnaround isn't a technical deliverable, it's the proof that the subject is a *thing* and not a *picture of a thing*. That's the flip from Project A, where the space held the person. Here the person has to hold the space in your head, from every side. That's the 60/40 tilt, and it lands on the thinking about form, not the rendering of one angle.

**The demo:** I'll take a rough lump and block it into a subject, and I want you to watch me *refuse* to detail. I'll build the volumes, the head, the mass, the base, and I'll keep turning it, front, three-quarter, side, back, and I'll check the silhouette at every turn. And I'll show you the one move that decides whether it holds: the **overall silhouette**, the outer shape of the whole subject as one shape, and whether that shape is *legible* from every angle. A good silhouette is a subject you can recognize in a crowd. A bad silhouette is a subject you can only recognize when you already know it's there. That's the test, and it's the one B1 is checking.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Figure Drawing: Design and Invention* by Michael Hampton, **Chapter 1, "Gesture Drawing."** The about-to pose and the wrapping line are the two ideas that keep a subject's volume *alive* in a turnaround. A wrapping line is a single curve that wraps around the mass, and it's the fastest way to check that the side and the back are still connected to the front. The center of gravity is the same idea that will keep your subject standing, and it's the reason a funpack that's balanced reads as *real* and one that's not reads as *pasted on*. Worth a pass before B1.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Framed Ink: Drawing and Composition for Visual Storytellers* by Marcos Mateu-Mestre, **Chapter 5, "Character Design,"** and specifically the **overall silhouette** and **dynamics of expression**. The overall silhouette is the single most important idea in that chapter for a funpack, because it's the test of whether your subject reads as one shape from every angle. The dynamics of expression is the same idea applied to the face, and it's the seed of next week's work, so a light read now pays off tomorrow. It's a short chapter.

But a subject with one expression is also a *trap*, because if the only face it has is the one that's already there, the subject can't *change*, and a subject that can't change can't carry a beat. That's the whole reason for variants. You make two or three faces, and you pick the one that serves the sentence, and in doing so you prove the subject can *do* something, not just *be* something. get it?

The analogy is a word and its synonyms. A word is one thing. Its synonyms are the same thing wearing different hats, and the reason you have synonyms is so you can pick the one that fits the sentence. Your variants are the synonyms of your subject's face, and the test is whether you can pick the one that fits *this* beat, and say *why this one and not the other two*. That's the same move you made with the directional studies in Project A, and it's the same move you're about to make with the shots in Project C. One skill, three coats, and now it's on a face.

**Why it matters this project:** a *subject that leads but doesn't trap* (your Project B brief) leads by *expressing*, and it doesn't trap by *varying*. If it only has one face, it's trapped in that face, and it can't lead anywhere new. If it has variants, it can lead, and it can lead in the direction the beat needs. And the silhouette check is the guardrail that keeps the expression from *replacing* the subject, because a face that has to do the silhouette's job is a face that's hiding a weak shape. The silhouette is the subject. The expression is the subject's *voice*. Both have to be there, and the silhouette has to carry the weight. That's the 60/40 tilt, and it lands on the thinking about form and meaning, not the rendering of one face.

**The demo:** I'll take the built subject and give it two or three expressions, and I want you to watch me *check the silhouette between each one*. I'll make the face, then I'll turn it to the side and squint, and I'll ask, does the *outer shape* still read as the subject, or has the face changed what the subject *is*? If the face changed the subject, the face is too loud, and I'll pull it back. If the silhouette still reads, the face is the voice, and the subject is still the body. That's the check, and it's the one B2 is testing, because a subject that can't hold its silhouette under a face is a subject that can't be trusted to lead.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Framed Ink: Drawing and Composition for Visual Storytellers* by Marcos Mateu-Mestre, **Chapter 5, "Character Design,"** and specifically the **dynamics of expression** and **overall silhouette**. The dynamics of expression is the idea that a face *moves*, that it has a before and an after, and that's exactly what a variant is, the before, the after, and the pick. The overall silhouette is the guardrail we just talked about, and it's the same idea that decided B1, so a re-read now connects the two checkpoints. It's a short chapter, and it's the one to have open while you make variants.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Figure Drawing: Design and Invention* by Michael Hampton, **Chapter 3, "Head Drawing."** The head is where expression lives, and the proportion and the tilt of the head are the two levers that do most of the emotional work. A head that tilts is a head that's *about* something, and a head that's square is a head that's *neutral*, and that's a decision, not an accident. The chapter is short and it's the fastest way to find the lever your face needs. Worth a pass before B2.

beats.oneNewConcept:
**The idea: material direction and the day/night hero, so the subject *lives in light* and doesn't just sit in it.**

Here's the thing a blockout and a face can't do. They make the subject *hold together* and *mean something*, but they're still a shape with a voice. To make it a *thing*, it has to answer a question the light asks: *what are you made of, and why should I believe it?* That's the material direction. In Blender it lives in the **Principled BSDF**, and the two sliders that do most of the work are **roughness** and **base color**. A rough surface diffuses the light and reads soft and used. A smooth one catches it and reads clean and new. So the same djinn in tarnished brass reads as *lived-in*, and the same djinn in clean plastic reads as *just made*. One serves your sentence and one doesn't, and that's a *direction*, not a default. get it?

And the day/night pair is the test. A subject at day is a subject in its *home light*, warm, wide, the one you designed. A subject at night is the subject in a *stranger's light*, cool, tight, the one you didn't design. If the subject reads the same in both, it's a *thing*. If it reads in day and vanishes in night, it's a *costume* that only worked because the light was on its side. That's the whole point of the pair. One render is a picture. Two renders in genuinely different light are a *proof*, and the proof is that the subject is real enough to survive a light it didn't choose. That's the flip from Project A, where the space was the constant and the light was what you adjusted. Here the subject is the constant, and the light is what you test it against.

**Why it matters this project:** a *subject that leads without trapping* (your Project B brief) has to lead in *any* scene, day or night, warm or cool. If it only leads in the light you designed, it's trapped in that light, and the next project, where the camera puts it in a shot you didn't design, is where that trap shows. So the day/night pair isn't a render deliverable, it's the proof that the subject is *portable*, and a portable subject is the only kind that can carry Project C. That's the 60/40 tilt, and it lands on the thinking about the subject's *truth under changing light*, not the rendering of one pretty frame. Because to pick a material, you have to know *what the subject is made of and why*, and that's the same skill as defending the face. The material is just the face's argument, said in a different language.

**The demo:** I'll take a built subject and give it two material directions, and I want you to watch me *test each one against both lights*. I'll set the day hero, warm and wide, and check the read. Then I'll set the night hero, cool and tight, and check the read again. And I'll show you the one move that decides whether the subject is portable: the **focal part under the rim**. The rim is that bright edge where the subject separates from the background, and if the focal part still reads at night with just a rim, the subject is a thing. If the focal part needs the day light to be seen, the material is doing the silhouette's job, and the subject is a costume. That's the check, and it's the one the day/night pair is testing. right?

> **Aside (further reading):** *How to Render: The Fundamentals of Light and Shadow and Reflectivity* by Scott Robertson and Thomas Bertling, **Chapter 2, "Light Types and Casting Shadows."** The hard/soft, rim, and occlusion vocabulary is the exact vocabulary the day/night pair uses. A subject with a strong rim at night is a subject that *separates*, and that's the whole test. A 1-2-3 read, bright, mid, dark, the Chapter 3a idea, is the fastest way to check whether the subject is still legible under the light it didn't choose. Worth a pass before you render the pair.

> **Aside (further reading):** *3D Environment Design with Blender* by Abdelilah Hamdani, **Chapter 2, "The Basics of Realistic Texturing in Blender."** The base-color, roughness, and metallic ideas are the vocabulary for *why* a surface reads as one material or another, and it's the same vocabulary you used in Project A, now on a subject instead of a room. Roughness does most of the work, a rough surface diffuses the light and a smooth one catches it, and that's the difference between a default and a decision. It's a recent edition, so closer to 5.x than the older books. Use it for the reasoning, not as a click map.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Color and Light* by James Gurney, **Chapter 7, "Color Relationships."** The warm/cool and the reflected-color ideas are the vocabulary for the night hero, because a subject at night isn't black, it's *lit by whatever's around it*, and the reflected color is the cheapest way to keep it reading as a thing in a dark frame. If your night hero is just a dark version of the day one, the color relationships are the fix, and they're the reason the pair is a test and not two of the same render. Stable ideas, any edition.

beats.oneNewConcept:
**The idea: the delivery is a defense, and the talk-through is a graded deliverable.**

Here's the thing about a delivery that's not obvious until you're standing in front of it. The render, the funpack, the silhouette, the pair, they're all *proof*, and proof is good, but proof doesn't *argue*. The argument is the talk-through, the two or three minutes where you say *what this subject is about, why this material and not the other, why this face and not the other two, and why this light and not the other one*. And that talk-through is a *graded deliverable*, not a garnish, because a subject you can't defend is a subject you don't understand, and a subject you don't understand is a subject you can't carry into Project C. get it?

The analogy is a thesis, not a poster. A poster is one face, and it's pretty, and it says *look at this*. A thesis is the *why*, and it says *here's what this is about and why I made it this way and not the other way*. Your delivery is a thesis that happens to have renders attached. The renders are the evidence. The talk-through is the argument. And the argument is the half that carries you, because a subject with a strong argument and a rough render is a subject I can help you finish, and a subject with a weak argument and a beautiful render is a subject I can't, because the beauty is the tool and the argument is you, and only one of those is yours. That's the 60/40 tilt, and it lands here, on the thinking, not the rendering, and the talk-through is the proof that the thinking is real.

**Why it matters this project:** a *subject that leads without trapping* (your Project B brief) has to lead in *any* scene, and the only proof of that is that you can say *why it leads* when the scene is one you didn't design. If you can't defend the subject in a room, you can't defend it in a shot, and Project C is a shot. So the delivery isn't the end of Project B, it's the *bridge* to Project C, and the talk-through is the plank you walk across. Because to defend a subject, you have to know *what it's about and why*, and that's the same skill as blocking a scene, because a scene is a subject that's bigger, and the *about* is the same move, just at a different scale. That's the 60/40 tilt, and it lands on the thinking, and the talk-through is where the thinking shows.

**The demo:** I'll take a finished subject and do a live talk-through, and I want you to watch my *structure*, not my confidence. I'll open with the one-sentence *what it's about*. Then I'll say *why this material and not the other*, one line. Then *why this face and not the other two*, one line. Then *why this light and not the other one*, one line. Four lines, one decision each, and then I'll stop, because the renders are the proof and the lines are the argument. And I'll show you the one move that decides whether the defense lands: the *why this one and not the other* sentence, the same sentence you've written four times now, in the directional studies, in the variants, in the material, and in the light. It's not a coincidence. It's the same skill, four coats, and the delivery is where all four show up at once. right?

> **Aside (further reading):** *Framed Ink: Drawing and Composition for Visual Storytellers* by Marcos Mateu-Mestre, **Chapter 5, "Character Design."** The overall silhouette, the dynamics of expression, and the about-the-character ideas are the vocabulary for the talk-through, because the four lines you're going to say, the about, the material, the face, and the light, are all *design decisions*, and that chapter is where those decisions live. If your talk-through feels like a list of settings, this chapter is the fix, because it teaches you to say *why* instead of *what*. It's a short chapter, and it's the one to have open before the crit.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Imaginative Realism: How to Paint What Doesn't Exist* by James Gurney, **Chapter 1, "Tradition."** The conviction there, that subjects you can't observe directly have been the mainstream of art since the Renaissance, painted with full conviction, is the same conviction your one-sentence defense is built on: a subject has to be *about* something before it can be *real*. That's the reason the talk-through is a deliverable and not a garnish. A subject without an about is a shape, and a shape can't be defended, because there's nothing to defend. Stable idea, any edition.

beats.oneNewConcept:
**The idea: the motivated camera, a camera that's there for a reason you can defend.**

Here's the trap that eats every scene in this course. The subject is good, the room is good, and the camera is *parked*. It's in a spot that makes the render look nice, and that's it. It's not *motivated*. It's not there because of the beat, or because of the subject, or because of the story. It's there because it looked good, and a camera that's there because it looked good is a camera that can't be defended, and a camera that can't be defended is a camera that can't lead. That's the whole reason the motivated camera exists. It forces you to answer *why here* before you're allowed to love the frame. get it?

The analogy is a journalist and a tourist. A tourist photographs the view, the one that looks good, and that's fine, it's a memory. A journalist photographs the *story*, the one that's *about* something, and the view is just the setting. Your camera is the journalist, and the beat is the story, and the subject and the room are the setting. The frame looks good because it's *about* the beat, not because the angle happened to be pretty. That's the difference, and it's the one C1 is checking.

**Why it matters this project:** a *scene as a story beat* (your Project C brief) only happens if the camera is *motivated*, because a beat is a thing that happens *to* someone, and the camera is the *someone's eye*. If the camera is parked, the beat has no witness, and a beat with no witness is just a picture of a room with a subject in it. If the camera is motivated, the beat has a witness, and the witness is the audience, and that's the whole of Project C. That's the 60/40 tilt, and it lands on the thinking about *why the camera is here*, not the rendering of one frame.

**The demo:** I'll take the subject and the room and put a camera in, and I want you to watch me *refuse* to move it until I can say *why*. I'll name the beat, the one thing that happens, and then I'll find the camera position that *serves* the beat, the one that makes the eye go to the subject at the moment it matters. And I'll show you the one move that decides whether the camera is motivated: the **motivation**. Does the camera's position *serve* the beat, or does it just *frame* the scene? If it just frames the scene, it's parked, and we'll find the motivation together. If it serves the beat, it's motivated, and that's the test, and it's the one C1 is checking.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Framed Ink* by Mateu-Mestre, **Chapter 3, "The Visual Message within a Still Composition,"** and specifically the **camera motivation** and the **establishing shot**. The camera motivation is the idea that a camera is *placed* for a reason, and that's exactly what you're doing. The establishing shot is the first camera in a sequence, and it's the one that sets up the motivation for everything after it, so a light read now connects to next week's continuity work. It's a short chapter, and it's the one to have open while you block the scene.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Dream Worlds: Production Design for Animation* by Hans Bacher, **Chapter 1, "Film Analysis,"** and specifically the **floor plan**. The floor plan is a top-down sketch of the scene, marking the main light sources, the character positions, and their movements, and it's the fastest way to find a motivated camera, because you can see the *whole* scene from above and pick the angle that serves the beat. It's the same idea as a top-down block in Blender, and it's the seed of next week's work, so a light read now pays off tomorrow. Worth a pass before C1.

oneConcept: the 180-degree rule, the line, the action axis, and why the audience *follows* when it holds.

beats.retrievalHook:
Two questions on last week, then a fast block.

- The camera is the journalist, not the tourist, and the frame is the story, not the view. In your C1 scene, what was the one thing the eye went to first, and *why* the camera was where it was? Name the beat.

**Fast challenge (2 min):** take your two cameras and imagine cutting from the first to the second. In your head, does the subject *jump* to the other side, or does it *stay*? If it jumps, you've crossed the line, and the audience will feel it even if they can't name it. If it stays, the line is holding, and the two shots are a *sequence*, not a *set of frames*. right?
beats.oneNewConcept:
**The idea: the 180-degree rule, the line, the action axis, and why the audience *follows* when it holds.**

Here's the thing about two cameras. One camera is a frame, and a frame is fine, but it's not a *sequence*. Two cameras are a sequence, and a sequence only works if the audience can *follow* from one to the other without a jump. The line is the invisible axis that runs through the action, the line between the subject and the thing it's looking at, or the line of the action itself. When both cameras stay on the same side of that line, the subject *keeps its direction*, and the audience follows. When one camera crosses the line, the subject *flips*, and the audience stumbles, even if they can't say why. That's the line, and it's the whole of continuity. get it?

The analogy is a conversation. Two people talking, and you're sitting on one side, watching both of them. You can see who's looking at whom, and the direction of the talk is *clear*. Now imagine you jump to the other side of the conversation, mid-sentence. Both people are still talking, but now they're looking the *other* way, and your brain stumbles, because the direction *flipped*. You didn't miss a word. You just lost the *thread*. That's the line, and it's the reason the audience follows when it holds and stumbles when it breaks. right?

**Why it matters this project:** a *scene as a story beat* (your Project C brief) only *leads* if the audience can *follow*, and following is the line. If the line holds, the beat has a direction, and the direction is the story. If the line breaks, the beat has no direction, and a beat with no direction is just a set of frames, and that's the trap. The line is the cheapest, most invisible, and most important thing in a sequence, because it's the thing the audience feels without seeing, and it's the one that turns a set of frames into a *story*. That's the 60/40 tilt, and it lands on the thinking about *direction*, not the rendering of one frame.

**The demo:** I'll take the two motivated cameras and show you the line, the invisible axis that runs through the action, and I'll move one camera across it, and I want you to watch the subject *flip*. In the first cut, the subject looks left, and in the second cut, after the jump, the subject looks right, and that flip is the stumble. And I'll show you the one move that decides whether the line holds: the **point of reference**, the one thing in the frame that *doesn't move*, the thing the audience's eye anchors to, and if the point of reference is consistent across the cut, the line holds, and the audience follows. That's the test, and it's the one that decides whether Project C is a sequence or a set of frames.

**A note for the turn you'll build next week:** the light / mood turn you'll design in Week 12 happens *inside* this continuity, not on top of it. The turn must not break the line or the point of reference, and that is the whole of the **hold what should hold** rule. The key direction can hold while the temperature turns. The point of reference holds while the mood shifts. The audience follows the turn because there is something constant to follow it against, and that constant is the line. So design the turn so it moves the *when* without moving the *where*, and the line stays the thing the audience trusts. That's the setup for C2.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Framed Ink* by Mateu-Mestre, **Chapter 4, "Composing for Continuity,"** and specifically the **line**, the **point of reference**, and the **jump cut**. The line is the idea that the audience follows when the cameras stay on the same side of the action, and the point of reference is the thing that keeps the cut *anchored*, the one element that doesn't move. The jump cut is what happens when the line breaks, and it's the exact stumble you just felt in the fast challenge. It's a short chapter, and it's the one to have open while you block the two shots. Worth a pass before C2.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Dream Worlds* by Bacher, **Chapter 6, "Camera Rules,"** and specifically the **180-degree invisible line** and the **jump cut**. Bacher's version is the production one, the one that's been on animation sets for decades, and the idea is the same: shots are allowed only along the line, and losing control of the logical sequence can *completely destroy a sequence*. That last sentence is the whole of this week in one breath, and it's worth sitting with. It's the same idea as the line in Framed Ink, just from the production side, so the two read together.

beats.oneNewConcept:
**The idea: the shot sequence, the contact sheet, and the light / mood turn that carries the story's emotional beat across the sequence.**

Here's the thing about a sequence that follows but doesn't *move*. The line holds, the subject keeps its direction, and the audience can follow, and that's good, but a story beat is a thing that *changes*, and if the light and the mood don't change with it, the beat lands flat. The turn is the light, the temperature, the palette, and the *when* deliberately shifting from beat to beat, so the audience feels the scene move. But it has to move *as one scene*, and that's the hard part. The line gives the turn its direction, the held constants give it its *one scene*, and the turn gives it its *when*. If the turn breaks the line, the audience stumbles. If it breaks the hold, the audience reads several disconnected days instead of one moment in motion, and that's the trap, and it's the one C2 catches. get it?

The analogy is a song, and this week it *modulates*. A song is a set of notes in the right order, and that's the melody. But a good song also *changes key*, a turn, a lift, a drop, and the turn is what makes the song feel like it's going somewhere instead of sitting still. Your sequence is the song, and the light / mood turn is the modulation. The line is the melody, the order of the notes, and it holds. The mood is the key, and the key turns. Both have to be there: the turn is the one that makes the melody *go somewhere*, and the held line is the one that keeps it *one song* and not several. That's the difference, and it's the one C2 is checking.

**Why it matters this project:** a *scene as a story beat* (your Project C brief) only *lands* if the audience feels it *move*, and the turn is what makes it move. If the turn is missing, the beat has no *turn*, and a beat with no *turn* is just a set of frames sitting still. If the turn is there and held, the beat has a *when*, and the *when* is the story, because a story is a thing that happens *at a moment, in a place, to someone, and changes*. The line gives it the *direction*, the turn gives it the *when*, and the contact sheet is the proof that both are there, and in order. That's the 60/40 tilt, and it lands on the thinking about *the turn*, not the rendering of one frame.

**The demo:** I'll take the two-shot sequence and give it a *turn*, and then I'll lay it out on a contact sheet, and I want you to watch the *turn* do the work, not the line. The line is the order, the turn is the *when*, and the contact sheet is where you see both at a glance. And I'll show you the one move that decides whether the turn works: the **named turn**. Does the temperature, the contrast, the palette, deliberately shift from beat one to beat two, while the key direction and the point of reference hold? If one frame reads as a disconnected day, the turn is the odd one out, and we'll find it on the contact sheet, because that's what the contact sheet is for. That's the test, and it's the one C2 is checking.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Framed Ink* by Mateu-Mestre, **Chapter 3, "The Visual Message within a Still Composition,"** and specifically the **quick read** and the **big, medium, small** hierarchy. The quick read is a composition you can take in at a glance, and that's exactly what a contact sheet is for, a *quick read* of the whole sequence. The big, medium, small is the hierarchy that keeps the read *clear*, the one shot that's the strongest, the one that's the middle, the one that's the setup. It's a short chapter, and it's the one to have open while you lay out the contact sheet. Worth a pass before C2.

> **Aside (further reading):** *Color and Light* by Gurney, **Chapter 3, "Sources of Light."** The color temperature, the hardness of light, and the inverse-square ideas are the vocabulary for *why* a mood reads as warm or cool, hard or soft, and that's exactly the decision you're making across the sequence. The color temperature in particular is the one that does most of the *when* work, a warm key is a day or a golden hour, a cool key is a night or a shade, and that's the difference between a sequence that reads as one moment and one that reads as several. Stable ideas, any edition.

2. **Do the final render.** The hero pass, **Cycles** if you have it, or a clean **EEVEE** pass if that's your tool, and the contact sheet, the quick read of the whole sequence. The render is the proof, and the contact sheet is the *quick read*, the one thing the eye goes to. Both are the artifact, and both are the decision, made visible. Save the file `c-scene_final.blend` and the renders `c-scene_final.png` and the contact sheet `c-scene_final-contact.png`.
3. **Write the one-sentence defense.** What is this scene *about*, in one line? And the why, why this camera, why this line, why this turn, and the one line that names the turn itself, what changes from beat to beat and why it's the right turn, and why the one thing it's not sure about is on purpose. That sentence and that why are the artifact next to the render, and they're the thing the crit will test first, because the crit is a conversation, and a conversation starts with a clear state, not a finished render. The render is the proof. The sentence is the decision. get it?
4. **Prepare the honesty.** The one thing the scene is not sure about, and the reason, fixed or left on purpose. Write it down, because the crit is where you say it, and saying it is the win, even if it stays, because a guess you can name is a decision you can make, and that's the difference between a finish and a hurry. That's the deal, and it's the one that's been the same on every gate this term, and now it's the whole thing.
5. **Save everything clean.** The scene, the cameras, the line, the turn, the contact sheet, the one-sentence defense, the honesty, all in one file, named like a human, with the collections clean and nothing orphaned. This is the file the term is built on, and it's the one that leaves with you, so keep it clean, because in a year, or a decade, someone is going to open this, and it needs to still make sense, and that someone is you. right?

**The on-hand tool:** the final is a **Cycles** render (or a clean **EEVEE** pass if that's your tool), and the contact sheet is a **2D app** or a **compositor** layout over the renders. If you don't have a 2D app, the compositor does the same job, less comfortably, but the *decision* is the same. The tool is the means. The *honesty* is the work, and that's the only thing the final is grading, and it's the one that decides whether the term is a finish or a hurry. right?
